Gray leaf spot (GLS), caused by the fungus Cercospora zeae-maydis, is considered the world's most yield-limiting disease of corn, and all corn hybrids have some susceptibility to it. The fungus survives the winter on infected corn residue at the soil surface, infection happens during long warm and humid periods, and symptoms are usually seen first on the lower leaves before the disease appears to move up the plant.

## Symptoms

Early: small, pinpoint lesions surrounded by yellow halos; the yellow margins are easier to see when the leaf is held up to the light. Early spots are about 0.5 cm wide and 1 to 2 cm long (0.2 by 0.4 to 0.8 inches), and the disease is hard to identify with certainty at this stage. Mature: narrow, rectangular, tan to gray lesions with blunt ends that run parallel to the leaf veins, because the major veins stop them from spreading sideways. Purdue Extension gives a mature length of about 4 to 5 cm (1.5 to 2 inches); Nebraska Extension describes mature lesions about 0.5 cm wide and up to about 7 cm (2.8 inches) long. The release of gray fungal spores on mature lesions gives the disease its name. Lesions can merge into large areas of dead tissue and, under severe pressure, blight entire leaves and even whole plants. Lesions on leaf sheaths and husks may be oval and are usually not diagnostic. On partially resistant hybrids, lesions may stay small with a round or jagged shape instead of the long rectangle. Symptoms may not be noticeable for up to two weeks after infection. Loss of leaf area from GLS can contribute to stalk rots and lodging.

## Conditions and how it moves

Infection occurs during prolonged warm (about 24 to 29 °C, 75 to 85 °F) and humid periods with more than 90 percent relative humidity; Nebraska Extension adds that the fungus needs at least 12 hours of free moisture on the leaf. Symptoms commonly follow long periods of heavy dew and overcast days. Hot, dry weather restricts the disease. The main spore source is infected corn residue on or above the soil surface; the fungus does not compete well in soil and rarely survives in residue buried below the soil. Infected leaf debris can still carry the fungus after one year and stalk and husk debris after two years, particularly in minimum-tillage systems, and damaging disease levels have been observed in Indiana fields with two-year-old corn residue. Spores are splashed by rain or blown by wind onto leaves, and wind may carry spores from a field with corn residue to neighboring fields. Bottomlands and fields next to woods, where dew lasts longer into the morning, are at higher risk. Late-planted corn meets its first infections at earlier growth stages, which can mean more disease and more yield loss.

## Yield relation (measured, not guessed)

The sources stress that the link between diseased leaf area and yield loss is not exact. If lesions reach the ear leaf or higher during the two weeks before and after tasseling, yield loss could occur; lesions that reach the upper leaves only later in the season cause less economic damage. A general Ohio State University estimate, reproduced by Purdue and Nebraska Extension, relates the ear-leaf area affected at early dent (R5) to approximate yield loss:

- 5 percent or less of the ear leaf affected: about 0 to 2 percent yield loss.
- 6 to 25 percent affected: about 2 to 10 percent yield loss.
- 25 to 75 percent affected: about 5 to 20 percent yield loss.
- 75 to 100 percent affected (leaf death): about 15 to 50 percent yield loss.

## Look-alikes worth separating

- Early GLS lesions can be confused with anthracnose leaf blight, eyespot and early common rust pustules; both cited extension guides name these diseases.
- Common rust: under magnification the rust pustules are visible, and breaking them open releases spores.
- Mature GLS lesions are quite distinct: tan or gray, limited by the leaf veins, rectangular, with blunt ends.

## Cultural management

- Hybrid choice: hybrid tolerance is one of the three main parts of GLS management. No hybrid is immune, but tolerant or moderately resistant hybrids restrict lesion growth. Seed company rating scales differ (some are reversed), so read the scale carefully. Weather remains the primary influence on disease development.
- Assess each field's risk: the best management plan depends on the level of risk in the field. Listed risk factors are a susceptible hybrid, continuous corn, late planting, minimum tillage, a field history of severe disease, early disease activity before tasseling, irrigation and a forecast of favorable weather.
- Break the residue chain: a one-year rotation away from corn followed by tillage is recommended; in no-till or reduced-till fields with a GLS history, a two-year rotation out of corn may be needed. Nebraska Extension reports that if residue covers 30 percent or more of a field that had GLS the previous season, damaging disease levels are likely in favorable weather.
- Continuous corn and no-till or reduced-till systems are at high risk because of the residue they leave on the soil surface.
- Scout before pollination: under favorable conditions symptoms typically appear two to four weeks before pollination; Purdue suggests scouting around V14, or just before tassel emergence, to judge disease pressure.

## What this article does not cover

This record intentionally contains no pesticide instructions. Chemical management is region-regulated and is handled only through separately reviewed, region-qualified records. If lesions are reaching the ear leaf around tasseling, take photos and consult a locally licensed advisor.

Common rust, caused by the fungus Puccinia sorghi, is present at low levels in most Indiana cornfields every year and is the more frequent of the two main corn rusts in the U.S., yet it rarely causes significant yield loss in field (dent) corn there. Ohio State Extension explains that highly resistant field corn hybrids are available and most have some degree of resistance. Rust matters more in seed corn, sweet corn and popcorn, which are more susceptible. In years with exceptionally cool summers, especially on late-planted fields or sweet corn, yield losses may occur when the leaves at and above the ear become severely diseased before grain fill is complete.

## Symptoms

Raised pustules, brown to dark reddish-brown (golden to cinnamon brown), oval to elongated and generally less than about 6 mm (1/4 inch) long, scattered over BOTH the upper and lower leaf surfaces. Pustules can appear on any above-ground part of the plant but are most common on leaves. Each pustule breaks through the leaf skin (epidermis), and the spores rub off, leaving a brown or orange stain on fingers or clothing. As the plant matures, pustules turn brownish-black as a later spore stage (teliospores) forms; in temperate areas such as the U.S. Corn Belt these black spores do not contribute to the disease cycle. If infection happens while the leaves are still in the whorl, pustules may develop in bands across the leaf as it expands. In Ohio, symptoms generally do not appear until after tasseling.

## Conditions and how it moves

Common rust prefers cool weather: Purdue gives about 16 to 25 °C (61 to 77 °F) for infection, Ohio State gives about 16 to 23 °C (60 to 74 °F) with high relative humidity, and UC IPM gives about 16 to 23 °C (60 to 73 °F) with relative humidity near 100 percent. About six hours of dew is usually enough moisture for infection. Young leaves are more susceptible than older leaves. The fungus needs living corn tissue and does NOT overwinter in crop residue in these northern areas; each year its spores are blown north on wind currents from subtropical and tropical regions where the fungus survives on corn. The alternate host, wood sorrel (Oxalis), is not infected in temperate areas such as Ohio and probably plays no important role in California. Under favorable conditions new pustules can form in as few as seven days, and repeated cycles can bring the disease to epidemic levels quickly. Late-planted corn may be at greater risk. Hot, dry weather limits the disease.

## Look-alikes worth separating

- Southern rust (Puccinia polysora): pustules are orange to light brown, small, round and densely packed, mainly on the UPPER leaf surface; the lower surface may show yellow flecks but very few pustules. Common rust pustules are brown to brownish-red, elongated and scattered on both surfaces. Both rusts can occur on the same plant, which can confuse diagnosis. Southern rust prefers warmer weather (infection at about 25 to 28 °C, 77 to 82 °F) and has greater potential to damage yields.
- Gray leaf spot: in hot, dry weather common rust pustules can become inactive and leave small dead areas that may be confused with gray leaf spot. A hand lens shows ruptured leaf skin around a rust lesion, which helps separate common rust from other leaf diseases.

## Cultural management

- Resistant hybrids: UC IPM advises using resistant hybrids to prevent common rust. Resistance ratings may not be available for all hybrids, so ask your seed dealer what resistance is available. In most years, hybrid field corn in Indiana does not need rust management; specialty corn may.
- Early planting: all corn plants develop age-related resistance, and planting as early as possible can reduce risk later in the season because leaves will be more mature and less susceptible when spores arrive.
- Scouting: because rust can reach damaging levels quickly, pay close attention to the level and timing of the first infections in susceptible hybrids, and check both leaf surfaces to tell common rust from southern rust.

## What this article does not cover

This record intentionally contains no pesticide instructions. Chemical management is region-regulated and is handled only through separately reviewed, region-qualified records. If pustules are increasing fast on the upper leaves, especially in sweet corn or seed corn, take photos and consult a locally licensed advisor.

"Corn leaf blight" does not name one specific disease in the sources behind this result. Purdue Extension describes northern corn leaf blight (caused by Exserohilum turcicum) and lists southern corn leaf blight as a separate disease that can be confused with it. The image class behind this result comes from public image collections that label it only as "leaf blight" (the CCMT dataset of maize photos from farms in Ghana, annotated by plant pathologists and virologists, and the PlantDoc collection of internet images) and do not name the causing fungus. A "corn leaf blight" result therefore does not tell you which leaf blight is present. More information is needed: compare the lesions with the description below, add close-up photos of several lesions, and have the diagnosis confirmed locally.

## Symptoms

Check whether the lesions match northern corn leaf blight, the leaf blight described in the cited Purdue guide. Early lesions are long, narrow and tan, running parallel to the leaf margins. They develop into long, oblong or "cigar-shaped" tan or grayish lesions about 2.5 to 18 cm (1 to 7 inches) long, depending on hybrid susceptibility. In humid weather the lesions produce olive-green or black spores, which give them a dark, dirty look and can be seen with a hand lens. Several lesions can merge into large, irregular areas of dead tissue, and lesions can also appear on the leaf sheaths and husks of susceptible hybrids. On hybrids with race-specific resistance, lesions are small and yellow and produce no spores. If the lesions look like this, see the northern corn leaf blight article in this app. If they do not, another disease may be the cause and local confirmation is needed.

## Conditions and how it moves

Conditions depend on which fungus is involved, so they cannot be stated for this label as a whole. For northern corn leaf blight, Purdue Extension reports that the fungus survives the winter on infected corn residue at the soil surface; infection occurs in moderate (about 18 to 27 °C, 64 to 81 °F), wet and humid weather and needs 6 to 18 hours of water on the leaf surface; spores are splashed or wind-blown to upper leaves and to other plants; and hot, dry weather restricts the disease. Yield loss could occur if lesions reach the ear leaf or higher during the two weeks before and after tasseling; if lesions reach the upper leaves only late in the season, losses will be less.

## Look-alikes worth separating

Purdue Extension notes that northern corn leaf blight can be confused with the following diseases, so an accurate diagnosis is important:

- Diplodia leaf streak.
- Southern corn leaf blight.
- Stewart's wilt or Goss's wilt.

## Cultural management

- Confirm the disease first: management depends on which leaf blight is present.
- For confirmed northern corn leaf blight, Purdue Extension recommends choosing a hybrid with moderate resistance and, because surface residue carries the fungus, a one-year rotation away from corn followed by tillage; a two-year rotation out of corn may be needed in no-till or reduced-till fields with a history of the disease.

## What this article does not cover

This record intentionally contains no pesticide instructions. Chemical management is region-regulated and is handled only through separately reviewed, region-qualified records. Because this label does not identify the specific disease, take photos and consult a locally licensed advisor for a confirmed diagnosis before any treatment decision.

Northern corn leaf blight (NCLB), caused by the fungus Exserohilum turcicum, is known for its long, cigar-shaped leaf lesions. Delaware Extension reports that severe outbreaks can cause 30 to 50 percent yield loss in dent corn if the disease is established before tasseling; Purdue Extension reports that hybrid corn yield could be reduced by as much as 30 percent if lesions are present before or at tasseling, and that losses in popcorn, sweet corn and other specialty corn may be greater. On hybrids with moderate resistance, disease progress is usually delayed enough to protect against yield loss.

## Symptoms

Symptoms usually appear first on the lower leaves and may move up the canopy. Early lesions are long, narrow and tan, running parallel to the leaf veins. They develop into long, oblong or cigar-shaped tan to grayish lesions about 2.5 to 18 cm (1 to 7 inches) long, depending on hybrid susceptibility. When humidity is high, the lesions produce olive-green or black spores, which give them a dark, dirty look; the spores can be seen with a hand lens. Lesions can merge into large, irregular areas of dead tissue that cover much of the leaf. Leaf sheaths and ear husks can also show lesions on susceptible hybrids.

## Conditions and how it moves

Infection occurs in moderate, wet and humid weather: about 18 to 27 °C (64 to 81 °F) according to Purdue and about 18 to 29 °C (64 to 84 °F) according to Delaware. Spores need 6 to 18 hours of water on the leaf surface. Symptoms are common after long periods of heavy dew and overcast days, and in bottomlands or fields next to woods where dew lasts longer. Hot, dry weather restricts the disease. The fungus overwinters on infected corn residue at the soil surface; spores produced there in spring are carried by wind, rain or irrigation to the lower leaves of the new crop, and spores from the lesions spread up the plant and to nearby areas by rain or wind. Lesions generally form one to two weeks after infection. Timing drives yield loss: if lesions reach the ear leaf or higher during the two weeks before and after tasseling, yield loss could occur; if lesions reach the upper leaves only late in the season, losses will be less. Purdue notes there is no clear relationship between the leaf area covered by lesions and the amount of yield loss. NCLB lesions can also contribute to stalk rot and lodging.

## Resistance, races and what you see

There are several races of the fungus, and symptoms vary with hybrid resistance. Susceptible hybrids develop the large, spore-producing cigar lesions. Hybrids with partial resistance typically produce fewer and smaller lesions with fewer spores. On hybrids with race-specific resistance (Ht genes), lesions are small and yellow and produce no spores. Spore-producing lesions still develop on hybrids with moderate resistance, so seeing them does not by itself mean the hybrid's resistance has failed.

## Look-alikes worth separating

Purdue Extension notes that NCLB can be confused with the following diseases, so an accurate diagnosis is important:

- Diplodia leaf streak.
- Southern corn leaf blight.
- Stewart's wilt or Goss's wilt.

## Cultural management

- Hybrid resistance first: Delaware Extension names hybrid selection and cultural decisions as the most effective practices. Plant resistant hybrids, especially in fields with a disease history, and check NCLB ratings with your seed provider; companies use different rating scales. Where NCLB is a chronic problem, Purdue suggests hybrids with race-specific resistance genes (Ht genes).
- Rotation: rotate away from corn for one or two years. Soybeans, small grains and vegetables are good rotation crops; avoid sorghum and sudangrass, which can serve as alternate hosts. Purdue recommends a one-year rotation followed by tillage, and two years in no-till or reduced-till fields with an NCLB history.
- Residue and tillage: tillage can bury infected residue and speed its breakdown. Continuous corn and no-till or reduced-till fields planted to susceptible hybrids are at high risk. Clean equipment before moving to a new field.
- Scouting: Purdue suggests scouting around V14, or just before tassel emergence, to judge disease pressure.

## What this article does not cover

This record intentionally contains no pesticide instructions. Chemical management is region-regulated and is handled only through separately reviewed, region-qualified records. If cigar lesions reach the ear leaf or above around tasseling, take photos and consult a locally licensed advisor.

Common smut, caused by the fungus Ustilago maydis, forms tumor-like swellings (galls) on corn ears, kernels, tassels, husks, leaves and stalks. The galls later break open and release black, powdery spores. It affects field, pop and sweet corn. It is generally not economically significant except in sweet corn, where even low levels make the crop unappealing for fresh-market sale and hard to process; large galls on stalks and ears can cause economic losses.

## Symptoms

Infected tissue turns yellow and galls form on it. Typical galls are fleshy and smooth, silvery-white to green, and spongy, with a greenish-white covering when young. Galls on leaves and tassels stay small (about 5 mm, 0.2 inch) and are often hard; galls on ears and stalks can grow to about 10 to 15 cm (4 to 6 inches). As a gall matures, its outer surface becomes papery and brittle and its inside turns into black powder (the spores); the gall then ruptures and releases the powder. Galls form within one week of infection and keep enlarging for up to three weeks before they mature. Infection stays where the spores landed; it does not move through the plant. On ears, smut tends to appear first at the ear tip, because those ovaries are pollinated last and pollinated ovaries are less susceptible.

## How it moves

Spores survive in soil and corn residue for several years (5 to 7 years, depending on conditions). They spread by wind, rain splash, equipment and insects, and through the manure of animals that have eaten infected corn. The fungus most typically infects ears through the silks; it also enters through wounds from insect feeding, hail, cultivation or machinery, and damage from animals or wind makes symptoms more likely. Infection is favored by warm weather: NC State gives 24 to 35 °C (75 to 95 °F) with humid conditions, and Wisconsin gives 26 to 34 °C (79 to 93 °F) with moderate rainfall, while Kansas State describes the disease as favored by hot, dry weather. Corn grown with high nitrogen or heavy manure, in low-fertility soil, or under drought stress is more likely to be infected.

## Edible galls and livestock feed

- In Mexico, immature smut galls are grown, sold and eaten as a delicacy called huitlacoche (cuitlacoche); NC State Extension states the galls are safe to eat.
- Kernels without galls on infected ears should not be fed to livestock, because they may contain high levels of mycotoxins produced by ear rot fungi (NC State Extension).

## Cultural management

- Avoid injuring plants, for example when weeding or cultivating, to reduce entry points for the fungus; scout for insect damage.
- Keep soil fertility balanced, especially nitrogen, based on a soil test; avoid high nitrogen and heavy manure applications.
- Irrigate to reduce drought stress.
- Once galls have formed, the plant cannot be treated. Remove galls before they rupture and destroy them (burn where local rules allow, or bury) so the spores do not spread and overwinter; this works best when neighbors do the same.
- After harvest, destroy stalks and debris as soon as possible and till deeply where erosion can be managed.
- Rotate with any crop other than corn: smut is limited to corn in nature, and longer rotations help more (a three-year rotation is better than a two-year rotation).
- Resistance: the sources differ. NC State states that no corn varieties are resistant, while Wisconsin advises planting resistant varieties where possible. Ask your local seed supplier about hybrid options.

## What this article does not cover

This record intentionally contains no pesticide instructions. Chemical management is region-regulated and is handled only through separately reviewed, region-qualified records. This includes any insect control intended to reduce wounding.

Maize streak virus (MSV) is spread by leafhoppers of the genus Cicadulina and produces narrow, broken, white to yellowish streaks running parallel along the leaves. It occurs throughout Africa, where it causes what is probably the most serious viral crop disease on the continent, and it is a major limit on maize production in sub-Saharan Africa. In East Africa, yield losses of 33 to 55 percent have been recorded under natural infection, and plants infected early usually produce no cobs.

## Symptoms

The first symptoms are minute, pale, circular spots on the lowest exposed part of the youngest leaves. Only leaves formed after infection show symptoms; older leaves stay healthy. The streaks often fuse into narrow, broken, chlorotic (yellow to white) stripes that may run the entire length of severely affected leaves; some virus strains cause red coloring. Infected plants have shorter leaves and are shorter overall; plants infected early become severely stunted, with undersized, misshapen cobs or no yield at all. Yield loss depends on when the plant was infected: infected seedlings produce no yield or are killed, while later infections cause proportionately less loss. In one report, infection at the second, sixth and tenth leaf stage caused about 55, 40 and 25 percent loss in grain weight.

## How it moves

The virus is transmitted only by leafhoppers: as many as six Cicadulina species, mainly Cicadulina mbila and Cicadulina storeyi. Leafhoppers pick up the virus from infected plants and pass it to healthy plants. Besides maize, MSV strains infect wheat, barley, oats, rye, sugarcane, millet, sorghum and many wild grasses. Leafhoppers breed mainly on annual wild grasses, and wild grasses are reservoirs of both the virus and its vectors. When crops mature or during drought, the strong-flying form of the leafhopper becomes dominant and migrates, including into irrigated crops, and can spread the disease over great distances. Epidemics are favored by staggered growing seasons, in which the virus builds up in early-planted maize and then devastates seedlings in later plantings, by dense wild-grass populations and by conditions that drive long-distance leafhopper movement. Outbreaks are often associated with drought followed by irregular rains at the start of the season.

## Look-alikes worth separating

The sources cited here do not describe look-alike problems for maize streak. If the streak pattern is unclear, take photos of young and old leaves together and have the diagnosis confirmed locally.

## Cultural management

- Resistant or tolerant varieties are probably the most effective and economically viable way to prevent streak epidemics; use them if available. Commercial MSV-resistant maize exists, but strong resistance has proven difficult to transfer into commercial maize, some "resistant" lines are better described as tolerant, and resistant types may yield less than favored susceptible varieties.
- Plant early in the season, when the amount of virus around is lowest.
- Eradicate grass weeds.
- Leave barriers of bare ground between early- and late-planted maize fields to reduce leafhopper movement; avoid planting maize downwind from older cereal crops; use crop rotations that reduce invasion by virus-carrying leafhoppers.

## What this article does not cover

This record intentionally contains no pesticide instructions. Chemical management is region-regulated and is handled only through separately reviewed, region-qualified records. This includes any control of the leafhopper vector. If streaks appear, take photos of young and old leaves together (the comparison is diagnostic) and consult a locally licensed advisor.

Bacterial spot, caused by Xanthomonas bacteria, is an economically important disease of pepper and tomato, of particular importance in warm, humid areas (UC IPM calls it relatively minor in California). Small water-soaked leaf spots turn brown, heavily spotted leaves drop, and raised, wart-like spots on fruit reduce its marketability. Seed is the main long-distance carrier: the bacterium travels inside or on seed and on transplants.

## Symptoms

On leaves: spots first appear as small, angular, water-soaked spots on the leaf underside and later turn brown. Sources describe the spots as small - roughly 2 to 3 millimeters in the review, about 0.25 inch (about 6 millimeters) in the UC guideline. On pepper the lesions become dark brown to black with a yellow halo, and they can look dark brown and greasy. The sources differ on shot-holes: the review reports no shot-hole appearance on pepper, while the Connecticut fact sheet says lesion centers can dry and break away, giving a shot-hole look. Do not rely on this sign alone. As spots multiply, leaves yellow and drop, and the lost leaf cover exposes fruit to sunscald. On stems: elongated, raised cankers. On fruit: circular, brown, raised spots with a cracked, roughened, wart-like surface. In transplant production, crowded plants, overhead irrigation, high humidity and high temperatures can lead to severe outbreaks on seedlings, and transplants can carry the bacterium into the field.

## Conditions and how it moves

High relative humidity and free moisture on the plant surface favor the disease. Symptoms develop 5 to 15 days after infection and develop fastest at 20 °C (68 °F) or above. Overhead irrigation, dense planting and handling wet plants help it spread. The bacterium survives inside or on seed and, for short periods, in infected crop residue and on weeds; it does not survive in soil once the infected residue has decomposed. It also survives between crops on volunteer pepper and tomato plants. Different strains exist: some favor pepper, some favor tomato, some attack both. Variety resistance works against specific races only, and strains able to infect peppers carrying a resistance gene (Bs2) have been isolated.

## Why bacterial, not fungal - a diagnostic habit

The visual signature on pepper is water-soaked spots that turn dark brown and greasy, with a yellow halo, plus raised, cracked, wart-like fruit spots. A photo cannot confirm the cause; if in doubt, have a sample checked by a diagnostic laboratory.

## Look-alikes worth separating

The sources behind this record do not describe look-alike diseases, so none are listed here. Use the sourced cues above, and treat a match as a candidate, not a confirmed diagnosis.

## Cultural management

- Start clean: use pathogen-tested (indexed pathogen-negative) seed and disease-free transplants; seed is the main long-distance carrier.
- Rotate out of peppers for at least 1 year, and do not follow pepper with tomato, eggplant or potato (Connecticut fact sheet).
- Manage volunteer pepper and tomato plants and weeds, which can carry the bacterium between crops.
- Use drip or furrow irrigation instead of overhead irrigation; avoid handling plants and working in the field while foliage is wet.
- Resistant varieties help, but resistance is race-specific; if a resistant variety still shows heavy spotting, record it and report it to an advisor.
- In transplant production, rogue transplants with symptoms, together with symptomless transplants within about 1 to 3 meters of them.

## What this article does not cover

This record intentionally contains no pesticide or bactericide instructions. Chemical management is region-regulated: it is handled only by separately reviewed, region-qualified records. If fruit spots or leaf drop start, take photos and consult a locally licensed advisor about currently registered options.

Blossom-end rot is NOT an infectious disease: no fungus, bacterium or virus causes it. It is a physiological (nutritional) disorder caused by a shortage of calcium in the enlarging fruit. Because the camera sees the symptom, the diagnosis label should name the disorder; the explanation lies in watering and plant growth, not in a pathogen.

## Symptoms

At the blossom end of the fruit - and on peppers also on the side of the fruit near the blossom end - a water-soaked spot appears and turns tan, brown or black, sunken and dry. The patch can enlarge and become dark, shrunken and leathery. Secondary pathogens may invade the affected area and rot the whole fruit; in dry conditions the patch often stays dry and leathery. It is usually an early-season problem: the first fruits are hit hardest, and incidence often declines as the season goes on. Peppers are generally less susceptible than tomatoes; it is most often seen on long pepper fruits, and larger, thick-walled varieties may be affected. Fruits in the rapid expansion phase (one-third to one-half of full size) are the most sensitive to water stress.

## Why it happens (and why soil calcium is rarely the whole story)

Calcium moves only with water in the xylem; it cannot move from leaves to fruit. Most of it goes to the leaves, which transpire far more than fruit. Anything that interrupts water supply while fruit expands fast - drought, swings in soil moisture, high heat, root damage, or slowed water movement in cool, cloudy weather or cold soil - can leave the fruit short of calcium. High levels of potassium, magnesium and ammonium nitrogen compete with calcium for uptake. This is why fruit can develop blossom-end rot even when soil calcium is adequate, and why adding calcium to the soil rarely fixes it. Foliar calcium applications are of little value: leaves absorb calcium poorly and it does not move to the fruit, so such treatments add cost without solving the problem. Recorded risk factors: inconsistent or shallow watering, drought stress, rapid growth pushed by excess nitrogen, root damage from close cultivation, low soil calcium and low soil pH.

## Look-alikes worth separating

- Sunscald: causes a whitish or translucent discoloration, not the tan, brown or black blossom-end patch.
- Secondary rot on old lesions: secondary pathogens can invade a blossom-end rot patch and rot the whole fruit; the first, dry blossom-end patch points to the disorder.

## Cultural management

- Watering consistency is the main lever: do not let the soil dry out while fruit is expanding rapidly, keep the soil moist but not wet, and irrigate before periods of high heat. If rainfall is lacking, water deeply at least once per week.
- Monitor soil moisture (for example with tensiometers or soil moisture blocks) rather than guessing.
- Mulch along the rows to reduce soil temperature and evaporation and to even out moisture swings; cover crops or compost that raise soil organic matter also help.
- Keep soil pH in the 6.3-6.8 range. Soil calcium additions rarely help unless a soil test clearly shows calcium deficiency; on high-magnesium soils with a pH below 6.5, liming may be useful.
- Feed moderately: match nitrogen to the crop's actual use, avoid high-nitrogen fertilizers like urea, and use nitrate forms of nitrogen rather than ammonium.
- Protect roots: avoid cultivating close to plants.
- Remove affected fruits as soon as symptoms appear.

## What this article does not cover

This record intentionally contains no pesticide instructions, and none apply: because the disorder is not infectious, no fungicide or bactericide acts on it. Chemical management is region-regulated: it is handled only by separately reviewed, region-qualified records. Input decisions belong to a soil-test-based plan. Take photos of several fruits, note the recent watering history, and consult a locally licensed advisor for input decisions.

articles.content:
Late blight of potato is caused by Phytophthora infestans, a water mold (a fungus-like oomycete), not a true fungus. It can infect potato foliage and tubers at any stage of crop development and spreads rapidly in cool, moist weather, so early recognition matters.

## Symptoms

The first signs on leaves are small, light to dark green, circular to irregular water-soaked spots, usually first on the lower leaves and often near leaf tips or edges where dew stays longest. In cool, moist weather the lesions expand rapidly into large dark brown or black lesions that often look greasy, frequently surrounded by a pale green to yellow border; whole leaves can be killed within a few days. Lesions also appear on petioles and stems. During active growth in cool, wet weather a white, mildew-like growth is visible at the edge of the lesions or along petioles - this is where the pathogen produces spores. In warm, dry weather the lesions dry, stop producing spores and turn tan. Severely infected fields often produce a distinct odor. On tubers: irregular, slightly sunken patches, brown to purplish on the skin (less obvious on russet and red-skinned varieties), with a tan to reddish-brown, dry, granular rot under the skin, usually less than 1/2 inch (about 1.3 cm) deep.

## Conditions that favor it

The pathogen is favored by free moisture and cool to moderate temperatures: nights of about 10-16 °C (50-60 °F) and days of about 16-21 °C (60-70 °F) are most favorable. Rain, dew and sprinkler irrigation all supply the water it needs; infection requires about 12 hours of free moisture, and a new disease cycle can occur every five to seven days. Hot, dry weather slows it. Spores travel short distances in rain and very long distances on the wind, and spores washed from leaf lesions into the soil infect tubers. In North America the pathogen survives between seasons in infected seed tubers, cull piles and volunteer plants; without oospores it needs living plant or tuber tissue to survive. Where both mating types are present, a sexual spore that can survive in soil may form. Tomatoes and hairy nightshade can also be infected and act as sources of the pathogen.

## Cultural management

- Plant certified, late blight-free seed tubers; do not plant store-bought potatoes or tubers harvested from blighted plants the season before. Do not mix seed lots, because cutting can spread late blight.
- Destroy all cull piles and volunteer potatoes, and remove hairy nightshade and other host weeds.
- Keep developing tubers covered with soil.
- Avoid excessive or nighttime irrigation, and avoid planting areas that stay wet for long periods.
- Scout regularly, especially low, wet areas, field edges along tree lines and other spots that stay wet longest; destroy late blight hot spots quickly.
- Watch nearby home-garden and market tomatoes - late blight can move from them to potato fields.
- Confirm before acting: positive identification is made by microscopic examination of sporulating samples or by laboratory testing (PCR). Other tuber rots (soft rot bacteria, pink rot, leak) often invade late blight-affected tubers and can make diagnosis difficult.

## What this article does not cover

This record intentionally contains no pesticide instructions. Chemical management is region-regulated: it is handled only by separately reviewed, region-qualified records. If the symptoms match late blight, take photos and consult a locally licensed advisor about currently registered options.

Late blight of tomato is caused by Phytophthora infestans, a water mold (a fungus-like pathogen) - the same pathogen as potato late blight, able to move between tomato and potato. It can become active in cool, wet weather, and infected plants often decline rapidly and die, so early recognition and fast, simple steps matter.

## Symptoms

Leaves and stems develop dark, water-soaked spots that enlarge until the entire leaf or stem turns brown and dies; dead leaves typically stay attached to the stems. Under favorable conditions a white fuzzy mold appears on leaf undersides; it contains the pathogen's spores. Stem lesions are brown to almost black. Infected fruits develop shiny, dark or olive-colored lesions that may cover large areas. When infection is severe, a foul odor is produced. Affected plants often decline rapidly and die.

## Conditions that favor it

Late blight can occur at any time in the growing season when the weather is cool and wet; a return to hot, dry weather slows it. Spores travel short distances in rain and very long distances on the wind. Outbreaks are sometimes brought in with infected transplants and seed potatoes. Potato is the main host, and infected tomatoes can act as a source for potatoes: late blight can move from local garden and market tomatoes to potato fields. Weeds in the tomato and potato family can also serve as hosts.

## Cultural management

- Buy locally grown transplants or raise your own; for potatoes, use certified disease-free seed potatoes and do not plant tubers harvested from blighted plants.
- Choose late blight-resistant varieties if late blight is a concern in your area.
- Keep foliage dry: avoid overhead watering and avoid crowding plants.
- Pull out and remove plants with symptoms; seal them in a plastic bag, leave the sealed bag in the sun for about a week, then dispose of it with the household trash. Do not compost infected plants. This protects neighboring gardens and farms as well as your own plot.
- Remove weeds of the tomato and potato family (such as horsenettle, eastern black nightshade and jimsonweed) that can serve as host plants.
- Learn to tell late blight apart from other common tomato diseases, such as early blight and Septoria leaf spot, before acting; acting on the wrong name wastes the season.

## What this article does not cover

This record intentionally contains no pesticide instructions. Once symptoms are visible the disease cannot be cured. Chemical management is region-regulated: it is handled only by separately reviewed, region-qualified records. If symptoms match late blight, take photos and consult a locally licensed advisor about currently registered options while removing infected plants.

Septoria leaf spot, caused by the fungus Septoria lycopersici, is particularly destructive in seasons of moderate temperatures and plentiful rain, and it can reduce tomato yields dramatically. The fruit is rarely infected - the damage is to the leaves.

## Symptoms

It starts on the lower leaves, usually when the first fruit begins to form, and moves up the plant from older to younger growth. Look for numerous small (under 1/8 inch, about 3 mm), circular spots with tan to gray centers and a dark brown border; a yellow halo may develop around each spot. Small dark dots may appear in the centers - these are pycnidia, the fruiting bodies where the fungus produces spores. On the leaf underside, spots may look darker green or water-soaked. Lesions can also form on stems, leaf stalks and the calyx. As spots multiply and merge, leaves yellow and die, and whole leaves may become blighted.

## Conditions that favor it

High humidity, warm temperatures and wet weather favor it. Spores are mainly spread by rain splash, and splashing soil carries them up to the lower leaves. Water is needed for spores to spread, and workers, equipment or insects moving through wet, infected foliage can spread the disease. The fungus overwinters on infected tomato debris and on solanaceous weed hosts such as horsenettle.

## Look-alikes worth separating

- Early blight: lesions are larger and darker brown, with concentric rings; Septoria spots stay small, without rings.
- Gray leaf spot: also small and circular with a tan or light brown center, but the center tends to crack open or fall out. Most hybrid varieties resist gray leaf spot while many heirloom tomatoes do not, so on heirlooms the two can be hard to tell apart.

## Cultural management

- Rotate away from tomato for 2 or more years.
- Check transplants carefully for signs of the disease.
- Remove crop debris, especially tomato debris, and all infected plant parts at the end of the season. Compost diseased plant parts only with hot composting (pile above 120 °F, about 49 °C, throughout, turned two to three times).
- Mulch to reduce soil splash onto the lower leaves.
- Water at the base of the plants and avoid wetting the foliage; stake plants, space them well and remove suckers from the plant base so leaves dry quickly.
- Once plants are established and starting to set fruit, prune off the lowest 3-4 leaf branches; during the season remove infected leaves.
- Avoid working among plants while the leaves are wet, and clean tools and equipment after leaving a field.
- Control horsenettle and other weeds in and around the planting.

## What this article does not cover

This record intentionally contains no pesticide instructions. Chemical management is region-regulated: it is handled only by separately reviewed, region-qualified records. If symptoms match, take photos and consult a locally licensed advisor about currently registered options while starting the cultural steps above.

Bacterial leaf streak is the major bacterial disease of wheat. It is caused by the bacterium Xanthomonas translucens pv. undulosa (older publications call it Xanthomonas campestris pv. undulosa). It is carried mainly on seed: infected seed is the most important source of new outbreaks. When the symptoms are on the glumes (chaff), the same disease is called black chaff. It also occurs on barley, oats, rye, triticale and many grasses.

## Symptoms

On leaves, infections begin as small water-soaked spots or streaks; early streaks look translucent. They turn brown and grow into elongated, light-brown streaks limited by the leaf veins, which may run the length of the leaf blade. A pale lime-green halo may surround them. In wet or humid weather a milky, cream to yellow bacterial ooze can form on the lesions; when it dries it forms light-colored, yellowish, resin-like scales or granules. Leaf symptoms can give plants an overall orange cast. On heads, black chaff shows as dark, more or less parallel stripes along the glumes, more numerous on the upper part of the head. Awns can show alternating bands of diseased and healthy tissue (a "barber's pole" look). A dark brown to purple discoloration may appear on the stem between the head and the flag leaf.

## Conditions that favor it

Wet weather favors infection and disease development. The bacterium tolerates a wide range of temperatures (about 15 to 30 °C) and occurs in very different climates, from sprinkler-irrigated fields in temperate areas to high-rainfall highlands; in Nebraska it occurs mainly in irrigated fields. Within a field it spreads over short distances by splashing water, rain and wind, plant-to-plant contact and insects. Small injuries to awns and leaves from hail or wind may help the bacterium get into the plant, and frost has also been linked to outbreaks. Over long distances it moves with contaminated seed. Bacteria living on grassy weeds and volunteer cereals can add to infection during the season.

## Look-alikes worth separating

- Pseudo-black chaff (brown melanosis): a genetic darkening of glumes, stems and other head parts in some varieties, linked to a stem-rust resistance gene (Sr2) and favored by high temperature and humidity. It is not caused by bacteria. The sources separate the two as follows. Sharp, discolored streaks between the veins of the glumes, scattered irregularly over the head, together with plenty of leaf streaking, suggest the bacterium. Darkening of the stem below the head on the same (sun-facing) side of most stems in a field suggests melanosis. Cream to yellow bacterial ooze in wet or humid weather confirms black chaff. Ooze only forms in wet or humid weather, so a lack of ooze in dry weather does NOT prove the darkening is the genetic trait. If you are unsure, especially before keeping grain as seed, have a sample checked by a plant-diagnostic laboratory.
- Stagonospora glume blotch (a fungal disease) also darkens glumes. The bacterial ooze described above is the sign that separates black chaff from it.

## Cultural management

- Use certified, pathogen-free seed. This is the most effective step, because infected seed is the main source of the disease. Seed producers should consider testing their seed lots before planting. Seed should be multiplied in a disease-free area under dry conditions, without overhead irrigation.
- Manage irrigation so the crop canopy dries completely between irrigations.
- Highly resistant varieties are not currently available, but varieties known to be highly susceptible to black chaff should not be planted.
- Control volunteer cereals and grassy weeds.
- Crop rotation is of limited value, because seed is the main source of the bacterium. Working infested straw into the soil reduces the number of live bacteria in it.

## What this article does not cover

This record intentionally contains no pesticide or seed-treatment instructions. One source states that no pesticide effectively controls this disease in the field and that seed treatment alone cannot control it. Chemical management, including seed treatment, is region-regulated and is handled only by separately reviewed, region-qualified records. The seed and irrigation steps above are the dependable foundation.

Head scab (Fusarium head blight), caused mainly by the fungus Fusarium graminearum, is a major disease of wheat and other small grains. It causes yield loss, from sterile florets and shriveled, light kernels, and it lowers grain quality: the fungus produces a mycotoxin called deoxynivalenol (DON, also called vomitoxin) that is toxic to people and livestock and can lead to price discounts or refusal when grain is sold.

## Symptoms

Symptoms are confined to the head, the grain and sometimes the stem just below the head. The first noticeable symptom is usually bleaching of some or all of the spikelets while healthy heads are still green; part of the head or the entire head may bleach. As the fungus moves into the central stem of the head (rachis), spikelets above or below the first infection point may also bleach. During prolonged wet weather, look for pink to salmon-orange spore masses on infected spikelets and glumes. The stem just below the head may turn brown to purplish. Infected kernels, called "tombstones", are shriveled, chalky, lightweight and may look pink. Important: when infection happens late in kernel development, kernels may be normal in size yet still carry the toxin. Infected seed germinates poorly, and seedlings from it may be reddish-brown, weak and tiller poorly.

## Conditions and how it moves

Wheat can be infected from heading to the hard dough stage but is most susceptible at flowering. The most favorable conditions are long periods (48 to 72 hours) of high humidity with warm temperatures (about 24 to 29 °C); infection can also occur at cooler temperatures when high humidity lasts longer. As little as two or three days of light to moderate rain can favor infection. Because the disease depends on weather, how often and how badly it occurs varies from year to year, and losses are worst when plenty of inoculum, a susceptible variety and favorable weather come together. The fungus survives in crop residue, especially corn residue and also wheat and other small-grain residue; spores from the residue are carried by air currents to wheat heads. Early infections can produce more spores that infect later heads, especially in uneven stands with late-flowering tillers. The greatest risk is when wheat is planted into last year's corn or small-grain residue.

## Look-alikes worth separating

The sources used for this record do not describe look-alike diseases. The signs they give for head scab are bleached spikelets on heads that are otherwise green and, in wet weather, pink to salmon-orange spore masses on spikelets and glumes. If heads look discolored in another way, or you are unsure, take photos and have a sample checked by a plant-diagnostic laboratory or local extension office.

## Cultural management

- No single measure gives adequate control, especially in weather that favors the disease. Combine as many of the steps below as you can.
- Rotation: wheat should follow a non-host or less susceptible crop (for example soybeans or another broadleaf crop) whenever possible. Planting wheat into corn stubble greatly increases the risk.
- Residue: tillage that buries corn or small-grain residue reduces the amount of fungus that can infect the next crop. In minimum or no-till systems, spreading chaff and residue evenly, and chopping corn stalks into small pieces, may help residue break down faster.
- Planting dates: stagger planting, or plant varieties that differ in days to maturity, so the whole crop does not flower during the same wet period.
- Varieties: no variety is immune or highly resistant, but moderately resistant varieties are available. Choose varieties with some head scab resistance; ratings are available from local variety trials and seed dealers.
- Seed: plant high-quality seed. If a seed lot shows head scab symptoms, clean it and run a germination test before planting, and adjust the seeding rate to the result.

## Harvest and grain safety (this disease crosses into food safety)

- At harvest, the combine can be adjusted (higher fan speed) to blow out lightweight scabby kernels, but this will not remove all of them, because kernels infected late can still be fairly plump. Cleaning after harvest (for example on a gravity table) can remove more.
- Aim to dry infected grain to below 13 percent moisture. DON can keep building up until grain moisture falls below 13 percent, so late-harvested grain can have very high levels. Purdue describes two steps: below 15 percent to stop fungal growth and toxin production, then below 13 percent to prevent spoilage in storage. Do not mix infected grain with good-quality grain.
- DON is very stable: drying and storage will not reduce it, although it will not increase in properly stored grain.
- Scab in a field does not automatically mean DON is present, and DON can be high even when disease levels are low. Only a chemical test (a laboratory analysis or a commercial test kit) can show whether DON is present and how much. Scabby grain may be tested before it is sold or fed.
- Pigs are the most sensitive livestock and may refuse DON-contaminated feed or vomit; cattle, sheep and poultry are less affected. Ask a veterinarian or feed specialist about safe feeding levels. Limits for DON in food and feed are set by authorities; the sources cite United States FDA advisory levels, so check the limits that apply where you sell or feed grain.
- Moldy grain dust can cause allergy and breathing problems. Wear a good-quality dust mask when working around grain with a lot of scab or other molds.

## What this article does not cover

This record intentionally contains no pesticide, fungicide or seed-treatment instructions. Chemical management, including seed treatment, is region-regulated and is handled only by separately reviewed, region-qualified records. If you see bleached heads, take photos and consult your local extension office or a locally licensed advisor.

Leaf rust (brown rust), caused by the fungus Puccinia triticina, occurs worldwide wherever wheat is grown; in the central Great Plains of North America it is the most common of the three wheat rusts. It infects mainly the leaves, and in severe epidemics the leaf sheaths too. The fungus uses nutrients that the leaves, chiefly the flag leaf, would otherwise send to the grain, so kernels shrivel. Heavy rusting makes the upper leaves die early, which shortens grain filling and gives smaller kernels. It is most damaging when the upper leaves are severely rusted before flowering. Losses over large areas are generally light to moderate (about 1 to 20 percent), but individual fields can lose more than 50 percent, or be destroyed, when disease is severe before heading.

## Symptoms

Look on the UPPER surface of leaves first: small to medium, orange-brown pustules, round or slightly elongated, scattered singly and at random rather than in stripes. Under favorable conditions they can cover nearly the whole upper leaf surface. The pustules break through the leaf surface but, unlike stem rust, do not cause conspicuous tears in the leaf tissue, and they seldom go through to the other side of the leaf. As the wheat ripens, black pustules (telia) may form under the leaf skin, mainly on leaf sheaths and blades. Their spores (teliospores) matter only in regions where the alternate host of the fungus grows; no alternate host is known in the United States.

## Conditions that favor it

Leaf rust is most important where dews are frequent from jointing through flowering and temperatures are mild (about 15 to 25 °C). Infection is best at about 15 to 20 °C with at least six hours of free moisture on the leaf, such as night-time dew. The disease builds fastest in wet weather at about 20 to 25 °C; under these conditions new pustules form within 7 to 10 days after infection and the cycle repeats. In cooler weather (5 to 10 °C) this takes several weeks. Spores are spread by wind and splashing water; spores carried long distances between regions are generally deposited by rain. The rust fungi can grow and multiply in nature only on living plant tissue. Leaf rust survives between crops on infected volunteer wheat and on early-sown and late-maturing wheat crops.

## Look-alikes worth separating

- Stripe (yellow) rust: small, round, blister-like, orange-yellow pustules arranged in STRIPES on the leaf; it favors cooler temperatures (best infection at about 7 to 12 °C).
- Stem rust: orange-red to dark-red pustules that are oval to elongated and larger than leaf rust pustules. They form on stems, leaves and leaf sheaths, on both leaf surfaces, and occasionally on heads. They cause conspicuous tears in the leaf or stem skin, giving the pustule edges a tattered look.
- Two rusts can infect the same leaf at the same time, so identify the rust before acting.

## Cultural management

- Grow resistant varieties: this is the first control measure in both sources. New rust races can overcome resistance, so check current local variety ratings. Planting several varieties that differ in resistance and maturity time can help avoid total loss in severe rust years.
- Control volunteer wheat: it carries the fungus between crops.
- Pay attention to sowing dates: early-sown wheat helps the fungus survive between crops, and losses are more frequent in fall-sown wheat and in spring wheat near fall-sown wheat.
- Avoid excessive fertilization and irrigation.
- Scout fields routinely from early in the season to detect rust early. Pay particular attention to the upper leaves and the flag leaf, and follow regional rust reports and weather forecasts.

## What this article does not cover

This record intentionally contains no pesticide or fungicide instructions. The sources list fungicides as one control option, but chemical management is region-regulated and is handled only by separately reviewed, region-qualified records. If rust appears early and spreads fast, take photos and consult a locally licensed advisor.

Loose smut, caused by the fungus Ustilago tritici, occurs wherever wheat is grown. It is a seed-borne disease: the fungus lives dormant inside the embryo of infected grain, and infected seed looks exactly like healthy seed. The damage shows only when heads emerge. It is not carried in the soil. New infections happen only during flowering, when spores from smutted heads, blown by wind or splashed by rain, land on the flowers of healthy plants. This is why seed choices decide the next season.

## Symptoms

Symptoms are not visible until the heads emerge. The spikelets of infected heads are replaced by a mass of dark, powdery spores (described as olive-black in one source and dark brown in the other). Wind and rain carry the spores away, leaving a bare central stalk (rachis) with traces of dark spores and sometimes grayish remnants of glumes or awns. Smutted heads may occur in groups. The two sources disagree on other signs. One says plants may show dark-green, upright leaves before heading, and that infected heads emerge earlier, are darker and slightly taller than healthy heads. The other says only the head is affected, the rest of the plant looks normal, and infected heads emerge at the same time as healthy ones. So do not rely on these other signs; the spore-filled heads are the reliable symptom. Smutted heads produce no grain. Yield loss is usually small (about 1 percent or less) but can reach 25 percent or more in severe cases, and is roughly equal to the percentage of smutted heads. Grain quality is not affected, and infected seed germinates normally.

## Conditions and how it moves

Infection happens only during flowering and is favored by wet weather, high humidity and cool to moderate temperatures (about 16 to 22 °C). Spores that land on the flowers of healthy plants germinate, and the fungus enters the ovary and settles in the embryo of the developing seed. The seed matures and looks normal. When that seed is sown, the fungus grows with the plant and replaces the head with spores at heading time. So the smutted heads you see this season came from infected seed that was sown, while spores from those heads can infect neighboring flowering heads and so the seed for next season. When smutted heads become visible, it is too late for any control in that crop; note where they appear and prevent the disease the following year.

## Look-alikes worth separating

- Common bunt (stinking smut): the kernels are replaced by "bunt balls" filled with black spores, but the head keeps its shape. The glumes spread apart to show the bunt balls, which are rounder than normal kernels, stay on the head, and give off a fishy smell when crushed. Infected plants may be slightly shorter. Loose smut, by contrast, turns the head into loose powder that blows away. Common bunt infects through spores on the seed surface and, in winter wheat, also from spores in the soil.

## Cultural management

- Grow a variety resistant to loose smut: one source calls this the best way to prevent the disease. New smut races can overcome resistance, so follow current regional variety recommendations.
- Use certified, pathogen-free seed; this is an effective way to manage loose smut. The fungus is inside the seed and infected seed looks normal, so sorting seed by eye does not help.
- Only infected seed can produce smutted plants, so grain from a field where smutted heads were seen is a poor choice for saving as seed: it can carry the fungus even though it looks perfect.

## What this article does not cover

This record intentionally contains no fungicide or seed-treatment instructions. The sources describe seed treatment as a control option, but chemical management, including seed treatment, is region-regulated and is handled only by separately reviewed, region-qualified records. Ask a locally licensed advisor.

Powdery mildew, caused by the fungus Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici (older name Erysiphe graminis f. sp. tritici), is a white to gray, powdery disease of wheat leaves. It grows only on living tissue. It grows mostly on the leaf surface, feeding from the outer cell layer of the leaf. Early-season infections make the plant produce extra tillers that later fail to produce seed, and yield losses come from smaller and fewer grains. It occurs almost everywhere wheat is grown and is favoured by dense, thick stands, moist and cool weather, and high nitrogen fertility.

## Symptoms

Look at the LOWER leaves first: they are usually infected first. The disease shows as white to light-gray, powdery fungal growth, mostly on the upper leaf surface; some patches can also form on the underside of the leaf, and on stems, leaf sheaths and the head. Patches begin as small white circular spots, often with yellowing around them, and can join into large masses on the upper leaf surface. As patches age, the growth becomes denser and turns gray, and the tissue around older patches dies and turns brown. Severely diseased leaves collapse and die. In older patches, small round dark brown to black specks (cleistothecia) appear embedded in the infected tissue.

## Conditions and how it moves

Cool and humid, not hot: wind-blown spores start new infections from just above freezing up to about 30 °C (33 to 86 °F) in moist conditions (relative humidity 85 to 99%). The disease is most favoured at about 10 to 22 °C, and infection and disease development decline when temperatures rise above about 25 °C after flowering. With favourable temperature and moisture, a new disease cycle can occur every 7 to 10 days. The main spores (conidia) do not germinate in free water on the leaf, and water can make them burst; in seasons with frequent heavy rain, mildew can be very low because spores are washed off the leaves or burst. Spores are carried long distances by wind. Between crops the fungus survives on volunteer wheat and grasses, and in autumn-sown wheat as infections that show no visible symptoms over winter. Resting structures (cleistothecia) survive in crop debris, but in most environments they matter much less for starting disease than the wind-blown spores.

## Look-alikes worth separating

- Leaf rust: orange-red pustules that form where the leaf's outer cell layer ruptures, filled with spores. Mildew is a white to gray growth on the leaf surface, not a pustule breaking through it.
- Black specks in old mildew patches are cleistothecia embedded in the infected tissue; they are a normal later stage of mildew, not a separate disease.

## Cultural management

- Variety resistance first: genetic resistance is the cornerstone of an integrated plan. Resistance may be lost when new strains of the fungus develop, and growing the same variety over a large area can lead to new races, so check the current rating of your variety.
- Manage nitrogen: high nitrogen favours mildew. Use balanced fertility based on a soil test.
- Avoid high seeding rates, which increase mildew severity.
- Destroy volunteer wheat and other volunteer small grains in and around fields; they carry the fungus between crops.
- Scout regularly: begin when the first stem node is visible and continue at least until the flag leaf has fully emerged, so a build-up is noticed before the flag leaf and the leaf below it are damaged.

## What this article does not cover

Septoria tritici blotch is a leaf disease of wheat caused by the fungus Zymoseptoria tritici (older names Septoria tritici and, for the sexual stage, Mycosphaerella graminicola). Together with Septoria nodorum blotch, it affects more than 50 million hectares of wheat worldwide, mainly in high-rainfall areas, and yield losses of 31 to 53 percent have been reported for the two Septoria diseases. It moves from the lower leaves up the plant and is especially damaging when late spring rains continue after the flag leaf emerges. The disease can reduce both grain number and grain size; under severe epidemics, kernels of susceptible varieties are shrivelled and not fit for milling.

## Symptoms

Infections start as small yellowish areas that expand into larger blotches. The blotches are first light green, then light tan, then reddish brown, and end as grayish-tan dead areas. They are often limited by the leaf veins, but can also be irregular or elliptical. The identifying feature is inside the dead tissue: small dark specks (pycnidia, black to brown), often lined up in a ROW following the leaf's breathing pores. When wet from rain or dew, these specks exude jelly-like masses of spores, described as pinkish-brown by UC IPM and as white to cream by NDSU Extension. The disease moves from lower to upper leaves; under favourable conditions a new infection cycle occurs every 21 to 28 days.

## Conditions and how it moves

Moderate temperatures and wet leaves: the sources differ on the exact conditions. UC IPM gives about 16 to 25 °C with free moisture on the leaves and about 6 hours of leaf wetness for infection; NDSU Extension says the fungus needs more than 24 hours of leaf wetness and is most destructive at about 10 to 20 °C (50 to 68 °F). Moisture is needed at every stage of infection. Dry periods and warm weather limit infection and spread. Two spore routes work together: airborne spores (ascospores) released from the residue of previous crops start the first infections, giving a fairly uniform pattern across the field; spores splashed by rain from the specks then spread the disease within the field, giving a patchy pattern. The fungus survives between seasons on infected crop residue; volunteer wheat and other susceptible grasses can also be sources of the first infections. Because the airborne spores can spread over long distances, crop rotation does not prevent new infections arriving from elsewhere.

## Look-alikes worth separating

- Septoria nodorum blotch (also called Stagonospora nodorum blotch): lesions are often lens-shaped with a yellow-green border; the specks are scattered randomly, not in a line, and are more common on nodes, stems, leaf sheaths and glumes. Its infection of the glumes is known as glume blotch. It can also be carried on seed.
- The LINE of dark specks following the leaf's breathing pores points to Septoria tritici blotch.

## Cultural management

- Manage residue: leaving large amounts of wheat stubble on the soil surface increases the chance of an epidemic. Ploughing, removing residue (for example for feed) and crop rotation reduce the main source of the first infections. Rotation reduces but does not eliminate risk, because airborne spores also arrive from other fields.
- Volunteer wheat and other susceptible grasses can be sources of the first infections.
- Choose resistant varieties. A variety reported to be resistant in one country may be attacked by the Septoria population in another, so check local ratings.
- Sowing date: in California, UC IPM reports that the disease is most severe in early-planted wheat, which is exposed for longer to favourable weather, and that later plantings are less likely to be severely affected. Check local advice for your region.

## What this article does not cover

This record intentionally contains no pesticide instructions. Chemical management is region-regulated and is handled only by separately reviewed, region-qualified records. If blotches approach the flag leaf, take photos and consult a locally licensed advisor about currently registered options.

Stem rust (also called black rust or black stem rust), caused by Puccinia graminis f. sp. tritici, is historically one of the most important diseases of wheat. Losses are often severe (50 to 70 percent) over a large area, individual fields can be totally destroyed, and it can destroy entire wheat fields over a large area within just a few weeks. It infects stems, leaf sheaths, leaves and heads. Damage to the plant's conducting tissue means less nutrient reaches the grain, so kernels are shrivelled, and severe disease can cause straw breakage, so heads are lost at combine harvest. Damage is greatest when the disease becomes severe before the grain is fully formed.

## Symptoms

Pustules form on stems, leaf sheaths and leaves, and occasionally on awns, glumes and seeds. They are oval to elongated, orange-red to dark (brick) red, and larger than those of leaf rust and stripe rust. They break through the plant's outer skin and leave conspicuous tears, so the edges look tattered; infected areas are rough to the touch. On leaves, pustules break through on both surfaces. Pustules are single and scattered, not arranged in stripes. Later in the season, the pustules produce dark spores (teliospores), which gives the name black rust. Severe infections weaken stems, leading to lodging and shrivelled, prematurely ripened grain.

## Conditions that favor it

Warmth: of the three wheat rusts, stem rust has the warmest temperature requirements. It is favoured by hot days of 25 to 30 °C and mild nights of 15 to 20 °C with enough moisture for night-time dew, and it is most important where dews are frequent during and after heading. Spores need free water to germinate; optimal infection needs about 15 to 29 °C (59 to 84 °F) and six to eight hours of free moisture on the leaf. In the field, new pustules appear 10 to 15 days after infection (7 to 10 days under optimal conditions). Wind can carry spores over great distances, and rain is needed to deposit them during regional spore transport. Between crops the fungus mostly survives as mycelium or pustules on volunteer wheat. Barberry (Berberis) is the alternate host on which the fungus completes its full life cycle; spores from barberry are now a rare source of infection but were historically important in northern North America and Europe, and barberry has been eradicated in most US wheat-growing regions.

## What is at stake in race evolution

Stem rust races change. A race known as Ug99, which overcomes the resistance in wheat varieties grown in the United States and other parts of the world, was detected in East Africa in 1998. By 2012, at least seven races of the Ug99 lineage were known and had spread to various countries in Africa and the Middle East. Because new races can overcome the resistance present in current varieties, a variety's resistance rating can become outdated.

## Cultural management

- Genetic resistance is the backbone: plant varieties resistant to stem rust, and check that the rating is current, because new races can overcome resistance.
- Control volunteer wheat between crops; it is the main way the fungus survives the season without wheat.
- Where barberry is present, it can play a role in the stem rust life cycle as the alternate host.
- Cultivar complementation: planting several varieties that differ in disease resistance and time of maturity can help avoid total loss in years with severe rust epidemics.
- Avoid excessive fertilization and irrigation.

## What this article does not cover

This record intentionally contains no pesticide instructions. Chemical management is region-regulated and is handled only by separately reviewed, region-qualified records. If stem rust pustules appear, take photos and consult a locally licensed advisor without delay: stem rust can destroy entire fields within a few weeks.

Stripe rust (also called yellow rust), caused by Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici, has the lowest temperature requirements of the three wheat rusts. Losses of 40 percent can be common, with some fields totally destroyed, and severe losses result when heads are infected. It is a major disease of autumn-sown wheat in regions with cool nights, and of spring wheat planted next to infected autumn-sown wheat. A single infection can produce a stripe the length of the leaf.

## Symptoms

The first signs are yellowish patches on leaves. Small, round, blister-like, yellow to orange-yellow pustules develop in these patches and line up in distinct STRIPES on mature, upper leaves. Under favourable conditions, entire leaf surfaces can be covered with stripes. Distinct stripes do not form on seedling leaves. Severe early infections commonly stunt plants. Pustules can also form on the glumes of the head, and occasionally immature grain is infected. Later in the season, dark brown to black pustules (telia) form streaks on the leaves and leaf sheaths.

## Conditions and how it moves

Cool and wet: infection occurs from 0 to 25 °C and needs free water on the leaf; it can even occur beneath snow. Optimal infection is at about 7 to 12 °C (45 to 54 °F) with eight hours of free moisture on the leaf, and the disease develops best at about 10 to 15 °C (50 to 59 °F) with intermittent rain or dew. Cold slows it down: the time from infection to new spores ranges from about 11 days at a mean daily temperature of 15 °C to perhaps 180 days near freezing. During hot or dry periods spore production stops, but often restarts when cool, moist weather returns; hot summers and dry seasons are the greatest threat to its survival. Between crop seasons the fungus survives as dormant infections and pustules on infected volunteer wheat in most areas; in mountainous tropical and subtropical areas it can survive by moving up and down the mountain on sown wheat. Spores may also come from nearby fields sown earlier or from later-maturing fields. Wind-blown spores are the main way it spreads, and they can be carried long distances. In 2009, researchers at the USDA Cereal Disease Laboratory showed that barberry (Berberis) is an alternate host; where barberry is present, the fungus can complete its full life cycle.

## Look-alikes worth separating

- Leaf rust: orange-brown, round or slightly elongated pustules, single and scattered (no stripes), mainly on the upper leaf surface; tearing of the leaf skin is rare.
- Stem rust: orange-red to dark-red, oval or elongated pustules, small to large, single and scattered, on stems and on both leaf surfaces, with conspicuous tearing of the plant's skin. It has the warmest temperature requirements of the three rusts.
- Stripe rust itself: small, round, blister-like, orange-yellow pustules arranged in stripes, with no tearing of the leaf skin.
- Mixed infections are common: in the field, wheat is often infected with stripe rust and leaf rust at the same time; name the disease correctly before acting.

## Cultural management

- Plant resistant varieties. New races can overcome the resistance in current varieties, so check the current local rating of your variety.
- Control volunteer wheat, which carries the fungus between seasons.
- Seeding date is one of the listed controls for stripe rust; ask local advice for your region. Spring wheat planted next to infected autumn-sown wheat is at particular risk.
- Cultivar complementation: planting several varieties that differ in disease resistance and time of maturity can help avoid total loss in years with severe rust epidemics.
- Avoid excessive fertilization and irrigation.

## What this article does not cover

This record intentionally contains no pesticide instructions. Chemical management is region-regulated and is handled only by separately reviewed, region-qualified records. If yellow stripes are climbing toward the flag leaf, take photos and consult a locally licensed advisor promptly.
